NVIDIA Jetson Prices Jump Up to 101% — the $249 Orin Nano Super Is Now $399

July 21, 2026 crmaris

No announcement, no changelog, no blog post — just new numbers sitting on NVIDIA’s own pricing table, with increases running from 33% to 101%.

NVIDIA has repriced its entire Jetson lineup, and it did it without saying a word. Every developer kit and every production module still listed on the company’s US pricing table now costs more than it did a few days ago — in several cases twice as much. We pulled up NVIDIA’s own Jetson FAQ to check, and the new figures are there in plain sight, with nothing attached explaining why.

The change was first spotted by a reader of VideoCardz, and the scale is the surprising part. The Jetson AGX Thor Developer Kit goes from $3,499 to $5,499. The AGX Orin Developer Kit moves from $1,999 to $3,499. And the Orin Nano Super Developer Kit — the board NVIDIA built an entire marketing push around as the affordable on-ramp to edge AI — climbs from $249 to $399.

The biggest jumps land on the oldest silicon

The percentages get uglier as you move down the stack. The Jetson Nano module at 1KU+ volume doubles from $99 to $199, a 101% increase on a part that has been shipping since 2019. The AGX Orin 32GB module goes from $899 to $1,799, exactly double. Xavier NX 16GB is up 80%, AGX Xavier Industrial up 84%, and the AGX Orin 64GB module up 88%.

  • Jetson AGX Thor Developer Kit — $3,499 → $5,499 (+57%)
  • Jetson AGX Orin Developer Kit — $1,999 → $3,499 (+75%)
  • Jetson AGX Orin 32GB module — $899 → $1,799 (+100%)
  • Jetson Orin Nano Super Developer Kit — $249 → $399 (+60%)
  • Jetson Nano module — $99 → $199 (+101%)

Nothing on that list is a new product. Same silicon, same specifications, same board revisions. Only the price tag moved.

Memory is the obvious suspect

NVIDIA has offered no reason, so what follows is inference rather than fact. But Jetson modules are memory-heavy by design — an AGX Orin 64GB module is, to a meaningful degree, an LPDDR5 product with a GPU bolted to it — and DRAM contract prices have climbed far enough that SK’s chairman recently described the market as abnormal. Embedded modules are low-volume, long-lifecycle parts with very little room to absorb a bill-of-materials shock. When memory moves that far, list prices tend to follow rather than get eaten.

There is a second detail worth flagging: all three developer kits are currently marked out of stock on NVIDIA’s US Marketplace. Repricing a lineup you cannot presently ship reads less like opportunism and more like a company resetting expectations before supply returns.

Who this actually hurts

Jetson’s role in the ecosystem has always been the cheap way in. University labs, robotics startups, hobbyists prototyping the thing before there is a company around it — that audience picked Jetson precisely because a capable dev kit cost less than a mid-range graphics card. At $249, the Orin Nano Super was an impulse buy for a research group. At $399 it becomes a line item somebody has to approve. And at $5,499, AGX Thor stops being the board you buy to evaluate and becomes the board you buy once you have already committed.

The competitive angle is not lost either. Qualcomm, Rockchip and a growing pile of Arm SBC vendors have been chipping away at the low end for years, and NVIDIA has just handed them a comfortable margin of headroom. Whether any of this proves temporary is the open question — and NVIDIA has not called it temporary. It has not called it anything.
